subject: get_profile() calculates air temperatures at heights above reference height are the same

messages.author: 9758bf7788372487
messages.subject: get_profile() calculates air temperatures at heights above reference height are the same
parts:
Hello Michael,

I find that if heights are higher than reference height, air temperatures (and other variables) at each height calculated by get_profile()  are the same. It doesn't make sense when canopy height is higher than reference height. I borrow example code to test it.
'''
RUF <- 0.004 # choose a roughness height
micro <- micro_global(RUF = RUF) # run with defaults other than roughness height (Madison, Wisconsin)
dates <- micro$dates # extract mock dates (units of months)
metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout) # above ground min shade conditions
soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil) # below ground min shade conditions
newheights <- c(1.3, 1.4) # m, new height needed (can be a single value or a vector of heights)
profile.out <- lapply(1:length(metout$TALOC),
                      function(x){get_profile(Refhyt = 1.2, # needs to be what micro_global uses as Refhyt
                                              RUF = RUF,
                                              heights = newheights,
                                              TAREF = metout$TAREF[x],
                                              VREF = metout$VREF[x],
                                              RH = metout$RH[x],
                                              D0cm = soil$D0cm[x],
                                              ZEN = metout$ZEN[x])}) # run get_profile across all times at new height
profile.out1 <- do.call("rbind", lapply(profile.out, data.frame)) # turn results into data frame
newheight.out <- subset(profile.out1, heights == newheights[2])
plot(dates, metout$TALOC, ylab = 'air temperature, deg C', type = 'l')
points(dates, profile.out1$TAs[profile.out1$heights == newheights[1]], type = 'l', lty = 2, col='red')
points(dates, profile.out1$TAs[profile.out1$heights == newheights[2]], type = 'l', lty = 3, col='blue')
'''

Thank you in advance for your time.

Best regards,
Junqi

messages.author: 6cec8ea3702ece93
messages.subject: Re: get_profile() calculates air temperatures at heights above reference height are the same
parts:
Hi Junqi,

That is the expected behaviour - air temperatures are just capped at the same value above the reference height by that function. The wind speed is the only thing that will change above that height (and it does subtly if you have a look at the output of your example). 

Note that the microclimate model of NicheMapR is designed for considering open habitats, not environments under forest canopies. You used a roughness height of 0.004 m which is a good value for typical open grassland or an area with occasional shrubs. You would need higher values of the roughness height to simulate taller vegetation, but it won't allow the local height to be under the roughness height. You can interpolate after the microclimate runs between the predicted soil surface temperature and the 'TALOC' value but not with the get-profile function because that is using exactly the same equations as are used internally to the NicheMapR microclimate model.

Ilya Maclean's package microclimc is focused on canopy conditions and might be useful to you. Or, depending on your question, I've found that you can get pretty accurate predictions of measured in-canopy conditions with NicheMapR by playing around with the horizon angles, shade levels and cutting down the wind speed. 

If you wanted to simulate an animal on the forest floor basking in sun spots you could alter what microclimate values go into the ectotherm model, e.g. simulating deep shade effects with the microclimate model and passing all those outputs to the ectotherm model except for solar radiation which you make for an open environment so you have an animal tracking a sun spot but the sun spot is traveling over shaded ground, if that makes sense. Below is an example of this (which may not be relevant to you but might be relevant to others):

# access to open and shaded conditions in an open environment (how it normally runs)
micro_open <- micro_global()
micro <- micro_open
ecto <- ectotherm()

dates <- micro$dates # extract mock dates (units of months)
metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout) # above ground min shade conditions
soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil) # below ground min shade conditions

environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(dates, soil$D0cm, type = 'l', col = 'red', ylim = c(-20, 50))
points(dates, metout$TALOC, type = 'l', col = 'blue')
points(dates, environ$TC, type = 'l')

# in a forest
micro_canopy <- micro_global(minshade = 90, maxshade = 100, hori = rep(80, 24), windfac = 0.2)
micro <- micro_canopy
ecto <- ectotherm()

metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout) # above ground min shade conditions
soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil) # below ground min shade conditions

environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(dates, soil$D0cm, type = 'l', col = 'red', ylim = c(-20, 50))
points(dates, metout$TALOC, type = 'l', col = 'blue')
points(dates, environ$TC, type = 'l')

# in a forest with access to sun-spots
micro <- micro_canopy
micro$metout[, 13] <- micro_open$metout[, 13] # change solar to that of open environment
micro$shadmet[, 13] <- micro_open$metout[, 13] # change solar to that of open environment
ecto <- ectotherm(minshades = micro$minshade * 0) # allow access to unshaded solar

metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout) # above ground min shade conditions
soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil) # below ground min shade conditions

environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(dates, soil$D0cm, type = 'l', col = 'red', ylim = c(-20, 50))
points(dates, metout$TALOC, type = 'l', col = 'blue')
points(dates, environ$TC, type = 'l')

All the best,
Mike

parts:
A quick relevant note: Ilya has been slowly moving point-based microclimate modeling in vegetated systems from microclimc to micropoint. microclimc is still fully functional but in a few years one might be better off with micropoint (which will feed in more directly to microclimf), once we've caught the bugs.

Best,
Dave

parts:
Hi Junqi,

There hasn't been any comparative testing of the microclimc model to the NicheMapR microclimate model in forested environments so it isn't clear when one approach is better than the other - perhaps you could have a go at this. 

I presume you plotted the 1.1 m prediction (TALOC) against the measured temp. It will probably be almost identical to the TAREF output, which is the elevation-corrected ERA5 'surface temperature' data. You're not going to see the advantages of using the microclimate model until you compute the temperature of an object under the canopy, because that will incorporate radiation, wind speed and humidity effects. It looks like you might have some solar radiation on your measurement device at times - where does the data come from? You could try running the ectotherm model to simulate the device, e.g. put in the properties of the logger, set the horizon angles so that it would only get sun around midday (horizon angles around say 80 degrees), and see if it captures the spikes.

If you're far from the coast I'd set coastal to F and might also be worth turning off the CAD effects to save compute time.

All the best,
Mike

On microclimc + NicheMapR comparisons: when we were performing validation for the microclimc paper, there was some comparative testing between microclimc and NicheMapR in forested environments, and I've done some comparisons since (unpublished) – generally microclimc does better in forests but both perform well, so indeed further comparisons would be great. Of note is that the steady-state mode of microclimc (useful for time steps of an hour or longer, which includes most ecological applications) also alreadly incorporates NicheMapR's efficiency and accuracy for calculating soil moisture and temperature, including underneath snow. See the function microclimc::runwithNMR() and the microclimc paper (attached) for details.

Maclean, I. M. D., & Klinges, D. H. (2021). Microclimc: A mechanistic model of above, below and within-canopy microclimate. Ecological Modelling, 451, 109567. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2021.109567

在2025年3月8日星期六 UTC+8 06:58:54<NicheMapR> 写道：
Hi Junqi,

That is the expected behaviour - air temperatures are just capped at the same value above the reference height by that function. The wind speed is the only thing that will change above that height (and it does subtly if you have a look at the output of your example). 

Note that the microclimate model of NicheMapR is designed for considering open habitats, not environments under forest canopies. You used a roughness height of 0.004 m which is a good value for typical open grassland or an area with occasional shrubs. You would need higher values of the roughness height to simulate taller vegetation, but it won't allow the local height to be under the roughness height. You can interpolate after the microclimate runs between the predicted soil surface temperature and the 'TALOC' value but not with the get-profile function because that is using exactly the same equations as are used internally to the NicheMapR microclimate model.

Ilya Maclean's package microclimc is focused on canopy conditions and might be useful to you. Or, depending on your question, I've found that you can get pretty accurate predictions of measured in-canopy conditions with NicheMapR by playing around with the horizon angles, shade levels and cutting down the wind speed. 

If you wanted to simulate an animal on the forest floor basking in sun spots you could alter what microclimate values go into the ectotherm model, e.g. simulating deep shade effects with the microclimate model and passing all those outputs to the ectotherm model except for solar radiation which you make for an open environment so you have an animal tracking a sun spot but the sun spot is traveling over shaded ground, if that makes sense. Below is an example of this (which may not be relevant to you but might be relevant to others):

# access to open and shaded conditions in an open environment (how it normally runs)
micro_open <- micro_global()
micro <- micro_open
ecto <- ectotherm()

dates <- micro$dates # extract mock dates (units of months)
metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout) # above ground min shade conditions
soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil) # below ground min shade conditions
environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(dates, soil$D0cm, type = 'l', col = 'red', ylim = c(-20, 50))
points(dates, metout$TALOC, type = 'l', col = 'blue')
points(dates, environ$TC, type = 'l')

# in a forest
micro_canopy <- micro_global(minshade = 90, maxshade = 100, hori = rep(80, 24), windfac = 0.2)
micro <- micro_canopy
ecto <- ectotherm()

metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout) # above ground min shade conditions
soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil) # below ground min shade conditions
environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(dates, soil$D0cm, type = 'l', col = 'red', ylim = c(-20, 50))
points(dates, metout$TALOC, type = 'l', col = 'blue')
points(dates, environ$TC, type = 'l')

# in a forest with access to sun-spots
micro <- micro_canopy
micro$metout[, 13] <- micro_open$metout[, 13] # change solar to that of open environment
micro$shadmet[, 13] <- micro_open$metout[, 13] # change solar to that of open environment
ecto <- ectotherm(minshades = micro$minshade * 0) # allow access to unshaded solar

points(dates, environ$TC, type = 'l')

Mike
